problem: How do you learn new technologies?
referenceAnswer:
When I learn a new technology, I usually start by getting a high-level overview. I often watch YouTube videos to understand what the technology is, why it exists, and what problems it solves.
If it seems useful or interesting, I dive deeper into each topic by reading articles, official documentation, and other resources. I like to break a large topic into smaller parts and learn them one by one.
If the technology is completely new to me, I usually begin with an online course to build a solid foundation. Once I have some experience, I prefer studying books because they explain the concepts and design decisions in more depth.
For example, when I wanted to learn system design, I first watched several introductory YouTube videos to understand the overall concepts. Whenever I found a topic I didn't fully understand, such as caching or load balancing, I researched it separately until I understood it. Finally, I try to apply what I've learned in a small project because I believe the best way to learn is by building something.

problem: Could you provide more details about the projects listed on your resume? Specifically, what was your role and what kind of impact did your contributions have?
referenceAnswer:
One of the projects that I'm most proud of is an AI interview preparation service.
In this project, the biggest challenge was improving the AI grading process.
At first, grading was processed immediately whenever a user submitted an answer.
This worked well when the number of concurrent users was small.
However, as concurrent requests increased, too many grading tasks were submitted to the thread pool at once.
I tried tuning the grading thread pool to scale quickly, but under high concurrency, the thread pool still started rejecting tasks.
This made me realize that immediate grading had a structural limitation because the system could not control the amount of incoming work.
So I redesigned it as scheduled grading. The system first saves the grading request, and then processes grading jobs asynchronously in the background.
As a result, throughput increased from 8 TPS to 231 TPS and p95 latency dropped from 20 seconds to 1.5 seconds.
From this experience, I learned how to design systems that stay stable even if traffic increases.

problem: Can you tell me about your current role?
referenceAnswer:
Currently, I work at an insurance tech company, supporting HR and organization-related ERP operations.
